title: Compressor Design — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Compressor Design's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: for the detector, the teaching retrospective gathered from the bundle, a walk from a sixteen-slot ring to a blind test of the page's 100, 500 and 1000 samples, and one ring read as a level and a delay at once; for the knee, a walk from the straight line to the question of whether the knee's harmonics ever stop. The ratio-and-slope wall belongs to Boundary-Crossing Instruments' face, not mine. I grow when the page's teaching retrospective gets its recorded evidence. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: The buffer adds the newest sample and subtracts the oldest, so the first sample in is the first out: first-in, first-out (FIFO), not FILO. Change 'FILO (First-In-Last-Out)' to 'FIFO (first-in, first-out)'. The check ran 384 samples through a 16-slot ring and every sample that left was x[n−N]², the oldest. The heading says FILO too: renaming it strands this face's section under 'Lost its place' until the manifest's heading is renamed with it, so change both in one commit and re-stamp.

'A sharp discontinuity in the gain curve is infinitely broadband … The smooth quadratic transition has bounded Fourier content.' Measured on a tone through the page's own curve (threshold −18 dB, 4:1, no detector): the hard knee is a jump in the curve's slope, not in the curve, and its harmonics fall about 12 dB per octave (11.6, 10.8 and 11.3 at three levels; 1/k²). The quadratic knee's fall faster, 15.6 to 19.3 dB per octave (1/k³ is 18), but they do not stop: at every width from 3 to 24 dB there is still a harmonic above −140 dB at or near the 255th, the top of the chart. Only a curve that is a polynomial in the signal itself has bounded content (a cubic stops at the 3rd); the knee is quadratic in decibels. Suggested: 'A hard knee is a sudden change in the curve's slope, and its harmonics fall only 12 dB per octave. The quadratic knee turns the slope gradually, so its harmonics fall 18 dB per octave: not bounded, but quieter, sooner.'

The region lines read 'gain = input' and 'gain = threshold + (input − threshold) / R', but what they give is the output level, as the code block's 'output =' does; the gain is output minus input. They also hold only with levels in decibels. Suggest 'output = input' and 'output = threshold + (input − threshold) / R', and 'levels in dB' once. The pieces use the lines that way, and the check matches them to the page's three regions with no gap.

'R=∞ … approaches a step function': the curve does not. Above the threshold it goes flat, a clamp (at −6 dB in, out is the −18 dB threshold). What becomes a step is its slope, 1 below the threshold and 0 above (measured 1.000 and 0.000). Suggest 'its slope approaches a step function'.

'Fractional R < 1 (expansion) … Expanders are compressors inverted': with R < 1 this formula expands only above the threshold (R = 0.5: +12 dB at −6 dB in, 0 dB at −30 dB in), which is upward expansion. The expander most studios mean works below the threshold, downward, and no value of R reaches it here, since below T − W/2 the output is the input for every R. It is the same algorithm mirrored to the region below. Suggest 'upward expansion', and a clause that the downward expander is the mirror.

pieces.file: Compressor Design — rich — the window you can hear.html
pieces.title: The window you can hear · a ring of slots, walked up to a blind test
pieces.caption: **Is 500 samples a time you can hear?** A drum loop made here from sine and noise, and a compressor whose only smoothing is a ring of squared samples and its running sum. Five steps: a sixteen-slot ring where you watch the first sample in be the first one out; the sum read as a level; the window's attack and release, one straight shape that ends after exactly N samples, beside slide~'s curve that never arrives; the window as a knob, with two measures, the gain's wobble on a 55 Hz note and the time it takes to grab a sudden tone (100 samples: 11.2 dB and 1.6 ms; 500: 1.4 dB and 7.6 ms; 1000: 1.0 dB and 14.9 ms); and last a blind test of the page's three windows, matched in level, labelled by ear and then revealed.

pieces.file: Compressor Design — rich — one ring two clocks.html
pieces.title: One ring, two clocks · the detector's buffer and Retrospective Delay's
pieces.caption: **One primitive at two time scales, heard.** One ring read two ways at once: the sum of what it holds is the detector's level, and the slot that leaves it is a delay. At the detector's 500 slots what leaves is heard as a colour, a comb with notches at 44.1 Hz and every 88.2 Hz above, not as a repeat. Stretched to 44 100 slots, one second, it plays back the phrase, and the level follows the phrase instead of each note. The last step hides the numbers and asks you to mark where the ring turns into time. It also holds a tension in the section: the window is time you can hear in what the compressor does, and below perception as a duration.
pieces.near: The same buffer, stretched to about a second

pieces.title: Three teaching beats · the bundle's May proof
pieces.caption: **The window heard in a room, as remembered.** Gathered from the bundle as it is. Its first moment is this section's claim told as a lesson: a window dropped from 1024 samples to 32 turns the compressor clicky, and 500 sits in between. It was reconstructed from memory, not recorded, and it says so. One tension to hold: the proof calls 1024 samples smooth and natural, where the page calls 1000 sluggish. The blind test above is one way to settle it for your own ear.

pieces.file: Compressor Design — rich — the knee in the spectrum.html
pieces.title: The knee in the spectrum · from a straight line to whether the harmonics stop
pieces.caption: **Does the quadratic knee have bounded Fourier content?** A 110 Hz tone through the page's own curve, with no detector in front, so the curve's shape goes straight into the sound. Five steps: the straight line and one spectral line; the hard corner, whose harmonics fall about 12 dB per octave; the quadratic knee, whose fall about 18; the page's four edge cases (R below 1, R = ∞, R = 0, W = 0); and last you answer whether the knee's harmonics ever stop before the numbers show. They fall faster than the corner's and do not stop; a cubic beside them stops at the 3rd harmonic.
